newsitem.title: GERMANY: German '97 tax bill clears mediation process.
newsitem.headline: German '97 tax bill clears mediation process.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 tax bill cleared parliament's mediation process on Thursday after heavy modification and was set to go to a vote in the Bundestag lower house of parliament later in the day.
Approval of the measure had been delayed for weeks by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), which holds a blocking veto on tax measures through its control of the upper house.

But the SPD finally caved in on scrapping the wealth tax rather than bow to a government threat to allow the bill to fail. Tax increases worth over eight billion marks were agreed last week to cover losses from the wealth tax.
Waigel, keen to get German finances into shape for European monetary union next year, welcomed the result.
"The government has implemented its main tax policy goals," he said.
The Bundestag was expected to vote on the tax bill in the evening, while the Bundesrat upper house is due to vote it into law at its last pre-Christmas session on Friday next week.
Despite the bill's approval, the centre-right coalition remains at loggerheads with the opposition over government plans to abolish company capital trading taxes in west Germany.

The SPD wants to impose a moratorium on introducing the tax in the former communist east. Waigel and coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) want to scrap the levy altogether, arguing that under European law it would eventually have to be imposed nationwide.
FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms offered to hold talks with the SPD over the Christmas parliamentary break to find a compromise on the issue.
